title: Test course-file findability through the cohort lifecycle
description: Use synthetic course materials in a test workspace to evaluate whether organizers and learners can locate a file during an active cohort and after it ends. Define five realistic find tasks, record completion, time and points of confusion, and provide a prioritized improvement brief grounded in the observed interface. Do not use actual learner files or publish unverified claims.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Measure file retrieval with a verified synthetic set at three cohort stages
acceptedWorkstreams.description: Inspect the test workspace first and place a small, clearly named synthetic file set only in locations the current interface actually supports. Give organizers and learners the same five retrieval tasks at cohort start, during an active cohort and after its end; log success, time, navigation path and confusion. Deliver the task script, observations and prioritized changes, separating interface evidence from assumptions. Never use real learner materials.

upvotes.reason: "Measure file retrieval with a verified synthetic set at three cohort stages" is a specific deliverable for this goal with a way to check it was done properly. it produces something checkable rather than an opinion, so the goal either moved or it did not.

upvotes.reason: Testing retrieval at three cohort stages with synthetic files is the right method, and the controls exist to test: Files has 'Search by file name' and a 'Deleted Files' view in the production code.
Concrete, scoped deliverable that directly supports the parent goal; feasible with public evidence.

The same five tasks and controlled synthetic file set across start, active and ended-cohort states directly test the lifecycle problem in this goal. Logging success, time and path separates a missing file from a findability or permission issue, while observing supported locations first avoids invented folder/archive features. Support is for this test design, not a claim that access after cohort closure works. Define the ended-cohort state and expected access with the owner before testing, and keep any unavailable state explicitly untested.
Directly tackles a verified acquisition or conversion friction point with clear, evidence-based scope.

rejectedIdeas.title: Split every find task into search-only and browse-only attempts, to show which path needs the fix
rejectedIdeas.description: A failed find task doesn't say whether search or navigation failed. Approach: run each of the five find tasks twice with different participants, once using only search and once using only browsing (channels, file lists, pins), on the same synthetic set at each cohort stage. Record success, time and the point of confusion per path. Done: a two-column result table per task and stage, and a brief that sends search failures and browse failures to different fixes (indexing and naming vs. layout and pinning).
rejectedIdeas.rejectionReason: This duplicates the accepted five-task retrieval study, which already records navigation path and confusion at each cohort stage. It also assumes a search function exists and adds a second-participant comparison that could confound results. Fold a search-versus-browse variant into the existing protocol only if the test workspace confirms search is available; otherwise record the actual paths and unavailable feature as observed.
